entries.summary: Karma, in Hindu, Buddhist and Jain teaching, is the principle that intentional actions bring results that shape later experience, including future lives. The three traditions explain karma differently. Jain teaching treats karma as a subtle matter that binds the soul, while Buddhist teaching describes karmic consequence without an eternal self.
entries.origin: Karma developed in Indian religious thought and is tied to rebirth and to the goal of release from it. Each tradition gives its own account of how karma works and what release requires.
entries.scripture: Scripture does not teach karma as a cosmic law of cause and rebirth. It teaches that it is appointed unto men once to die, and after this the judgment (Hebrews 9:27). Salvation is by grace through faith, not by the balance of deeds (Ephesians 2:8-9). Galatians 6:7-8 uses farming imagery about the harvest of living for the flesh or for the Spirit in this life. It is not a teaching of karma or of rebirth.

entries.summary: Reincarnation, or rebirth, is the teaching in several Indian traditions that a person or life-stream is reborn in new lives, with the next life shaped by karma. Hindu and Jain teaching hold that a self or soul continues through rebirths. Buddhist teaching denies an eternal self and explains rebirth as the continuation of a causal series of impermanent elements. Schools within each tradition differ on the details. Some New Age and esoteric writers also teach reincarnation.
entries.origin: Rebirth is central to Hindu and Jain teaching. Buddhist teaching denies a permanent self (anatta), so rebirth is explained by causal continuity, not by an eternal soul passing from body to body.
entries.scripture: Scripture teaches that it is appointed unto men once to die, and after this the judgment (Hebrews 9:27). Jesus told the thief on the cross, 'To day shalt thou be with me in paradise' (Luke 23:43), and Paul wrote of his desire 'to depart, and to be with Christ' (Philippians 1:23). These passages describe life with Christ after death, not a return to earth. The Christian view is that reincarnation is not taught in Scripture.

entries.summary: Nirvana in Buddhism and moksha in Hindu traditions are goals of release, and the traditions define them differently. Buddhist nirvana is release from craving and suffering, understood through the teaching of no permanent self. Moksha is liberation from rebirth, and Hindu schools describe it in different ways. In Jain teaching, liberation is the complete removal of karmic matter from the self.
entries.origin: Nirvana and moksha are goals of practice in Buddhist, Hindu and Jain traditions. Each is explained on its own terms and should not be reduced to a single idea of liberating the self.
entries.scripture: Scripture does not describe release from rebirth. It presents eternal life as the gift of God through his Son (John 3:16) and the hope of being with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8). Jesus said: 'I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me' (John 14:6). He also said: 'If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed' (John 8:36).

entries.summary: Catholic teaching holds that purgatory is a final purification after death for those who die in God's grace and friendship but are still imperfectly purified, so that they achieve the holiness needed to enter the joy of heaven. The Catechism of the Catholic Church calls this final purification of the elect entirely different from the punishment of the damned. The Council of Trent, in its decree on purgatory (Session 25, December 1563), taught that the souls there are helped by the suffrages of the faithful. The Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of America, an official Orthodox jurisdiction, states that the Orthodox Church does not believe in purgatory (a place of purging), while Orthodox churches pray for the departed. Prayer for the departed is therefore not, by itself, the Catholic doctrine of purgatory. The Westminster Confession (1646), a Reformed statement, says that beside heaven and hell, for souls separated from their bodies, the Scripture acknowledgeth none.
entries.origin: Catholic teaching on purgatory was defined at the Council of Trent (Session 25, December 1563). Catholic and Orthodox writers differ on its basis. Historians debate how the doctrine developed before Trent; this entry does not date that development.
entries.scripture: Scripture says that the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin (1 John 1:7), and that believers are justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus (Romans 3:24). Paul says that to be absent from the body is to be present with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8). Catholic teaching cites the example of Judas Maccabeus, who made atonement for the dead, from 2 Maccabees, a book outside the Protestant canon. Reformed and Evangelical readers take 1 Corinthians 3:13-15, which speaks of works tested by fire, to describe the testing and reward of Christian work at the judgment, not a cleansing after death, and find no cleansing after death beyond the work of Christ.

entries.summary: Catholic teaching holds that the saints in heaven, including Mary, can and should be asked to intercede for believers on earth. The Catechism of the Catholic Church (2683) says: 'We can and should ask them to intercede for us and for the whole world.' Orthodox churches honour the saints. Philip Schaff's English summary of the Confession of Dositheus, from the Synod of Jerusalem (1672), reports that the saints, especially the immaculate Mother of our Lord, and the holy angels bring our prayers and petitions before God. The Orthodox Church in America's official texts speak of communion with the Mother of God, the angels and the saints, and of prayer for the departed addressed to God. Reformed and Evangelical Christians hold that Christ alone is the one mediator, that believers may pray for one another, and that worship is due to God alone. The Westminster Confession (1646) says religious worship is to be given to God 'and to Him alone, not to angels, saints, or any other creature.'
entries.origin: The teaching on the intercession of the saints is stated in the Catechism of the Catholic Church and in the Synod of Jerusalem's confession, both cited here. The Westminster Confession states that religious worship is not to be given to saints.
entries.scripture: Some Catholic and Orthodox writers cite Hebrews 12:1, which speaks of 'so great a cloud of witnesses', and Revelation 5:8 and 8:3-4, where the prayers of the saints come before God. Reformed and Evangelical readers reply that Hebrews 12:1 describes witnesses to the race of faith, not persons who hear prayer, and that in Revelation 8:3 an angel offers the prayers of all saints to God. Scripture commands prayer and intercession for all people (1 Timothy 2:1), and names one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5). Reformed and Evangelical readers note that this verse does not forbid believers praying for one another, and they place the unique mediation of Christ at the centre. Hebrews 4:16 invites believers to come boldly to the throne of grace.

entries.summary: Catholic teaching calls Mary the Mother of God and of the redeemer, and the Mother of the Church. The Catechism (969) says the Blessed Virgin is invoked in the Church under the titles of Advocate, Helper, Benefactress, and Mediatrix, and (970) that her mediation in no way obscures or diminishes the unique mediation of Christ. The Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith's note Mater Populi Fidelis (4 November 2025) judges the title Co-redemptrix always inappropriate for defining Mary's cooperation, because it risks obscuring Christ's unique mediation. It says special prudence is required in applying the term Mediatrix to Mary, and that any talk of her mediation in grace must be understood as a distant analogy to Christ's unique mediation. The note records that a 1921 request for a dogmatic definition of Mary as Mediatrix was answered by approving a feast, not a dogma. Pope Pius XII defined the bodily Assumption of Mary in 1950 (Munificentissimus Deus). Philip Schaff's English summary of the 1672 Synod of Jerusalem's confession speaks of hyperdulia for the Mother of God and dulia for the saints. Eastern Orthodox texts checked here call Mary the Holy Theotokos; they do not use the titles Mediatrix or Co-redemptrix in the texts checked. Reformed and Evangelical Christians hold that Christ is the only mediator and redeemer, and commonly honour Mary as the mother of the Lord.
entries.origin: The note Mater Populi Fidelis records that the title Co-redemptrix first appeared in the fifteenth century as a correction to the invocation Redemptrix, and that the Second Vatican Council refrained from using it for dogmatic, pastoral and ecumenical reasons. The dogma of Mary as Mother of God was proclaimed at the Council of Ephesus. The Assumption was defined in 1950.
entries.scripture: Scripture calls Mary blessed among women (Luke 1:42), and Elisabeth calls her the mother of my Lord (Luke 1:43). Mary calls God her Saviour (Luke 1:47). At Cana she tells the servants, Whatsoever he saith unto you, do it (John 2:5). Scripture names Jesus as the one mediator (1 Timothy 2:5), and says there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved (Acts 4:12). Reformed and Evangelical readers reject titles that give Mary a share in redemption or in the mediation of grace, and the note Mater Populi Fidelis makes the same point about Christ's unique mediation.

entries.summary: Catholic and Eastern Orthodox traditions use icons in devotion. The Second Council of Nicaea (787) taught that the honour paid to an image passes on to what the image represents, and distinguished the honourable reverence given to images from the true worship of faith, which pertains alone to the divine nature. Philip Schaff's English summary of the 1672 Synod of Jerusalem's confession likewise speaks of the reverence due to images of Christ and of the saints. Reformed and Evangelical readers of the second commandment hold that images used in worship, and bowing before them, are forbidden.
entries.origin: The Second Council of Nicaea (787) defended the veneration of icons, and its decree is the main conciliar statement on the matter cited here. Reformed teaching holds that the use of images in worship goes beyond what Scripture commands.
entries.scripture: The second commandment forbids making an image in order to bow down to it and serve it (Exodus 20:4-5). Scripture also records God's command to make cherubim for the mercy seat (Exodus 25:18-22), so the question is the use and veneration of images, not every image. Nicaea II taught that honour shown to an image passes to what it represents, and that the true worship of faith is reserved for God. Reformed and Evangelical readers reply that Scripture gives no warrant for honouring God through images or for bowing before them in worship, and that the Father seeks true worshippers, who worship him in spirit and in truth (John 4:23-24).

entries.summary: Soul sleep is the teaching that the dead are unconscious until the resurrection. Christadelphian teaching states that all await resurrection in the sleep of death, where there is no consciousness. Seventh-day Adventist Fundamental Belief 26 states that until that day death is an unconscious state for all people. The Westminster Confession (1646), a Reformed statement, says that the souls of the dead 'neither die nor sleep, having an immortal subsistence, immediately return to God who gave them'. The Catechism of the Catholic Church teaches that each man receives his eternal retribution in his immortal soul at the very moment of his death (1022). The guide's own biblical evaluation, which is not a survey of any church's official teaching, is that the believer is conscious with the Lord at death and that the resurrection of the body completes the hope. Ecclesiastes 9:5 is read in its literary context before it is applied to this question.
entries.origin: Soul sleep is taught in Christadelphian and Seventh-day Adventist publications. The conscious intermediate state is the position of this guide, based on Scripture; the guide does not claim that every Catholic, Orthodox or Protestant body holds it in the same form.
entries.scripture: Ecclesiastes 9:5 says: 'For the living know that they shall die: but the dead know not any thing, neither have they any more a reward; for the memory of them is forgotten.' The book describes what can be seen and known 'under the sun', from the human side of life, and it does not stand alone: Ecclesiastes 12:7 says that the spirit shall return unto God who gave it. Advocates of soul sleep also cite Daniel 12:2 for those who awake. Paul wrote of his desire 'to depart, and to be with Christ' (Philippians 1:23), and of being 'absent from the body' and 'present with the Lord' (2 Corinthians 5:8). Luke 16:19-31 is a parable, and it must be read by its genre. Together these passages make the case that the believer is with Christ at death, while the full hope is the resurrection of the body.

entries.summary: Conditional immortality holds that immortality is given only to those who receive eternal life in Christ, and is not an inherent property of the human soul. On this view, those who finally reject God are destroyed rather than kept alive to suffer conscious punishment for ever. Jehovah's Witnesses teach that God will annihilate, or permanently destroy, the wicked, and that he will not keep them alive in hell in order to torment them. The Birmingham Amended Statement of Faith, which most Christadelphian congregations adopt, speaks in clause 29 of 'the final extinction of the wicked' after the thousand years. The traditional Christian view holds that the lost suffer conscious punishment for ever. Perazim has not approved a position on the nature or duration of final punishment, so the guide sets out both views and does not state one as Perazim's view.
entries.origin: Conditional immortality is taught in Jehovah's Witness and Christadelphian publications. The traditional view, that the lost suffer conscious punishment for ever, is the view that conditional immortality opposes. Each view is explained in its own terms.
entries.scripture: Advocates of conditional immortality cite 1 Timothy 6:16, which says that God alone 'hath immortality' (KJV: 'who only hath immortality'); Romans 6:23, that the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord; and Ezekiel 18:4, 'The soul that sinneth, it shall die.' Advocates of the traditional view cite Matthew 25:46, where the same Greek word for eternal describes both the life of the righteous and the punishment of the wicked, and Revelation 20:10, which says that the devil, the beast and the false prophet 'shall be tormented day and night for ever and ever.' Revelation 20:10 names three figures and does not by itself settle the fate of every person. The guide explains both arguments and does not decide between them for Perazim.

entries.summary: Religious pluralism is the view, held in several forms, that the religions are valid ways of approaching a reality no one religion has fully grasped. Philosophical pluralists hold that the religions point imperfectly to one ultimate reality. Radical pluralists hold that the religions are irreducibly diverse. Pluralism is not the teaching of Hinduism as a whole, or of every New Age writer. Christians hold that Jesus Christ is the one way to the Father.
entries.origin: Pluralism is a modern philosophical view, shaped by the comparative study of religions and held in different forms.
entries.scripture: Jesus said: 'I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me' (John 14:6). Peter said that there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved (Acts 4:12). These claims are exclusive, so the Christian reading does not allow that all religions lead to the same salvation. Scripture also teaches that God is known in part through creation (Romans 1:20). Christians may recognise truth and goodness in other traditions while holding that salvation is in Christ alone.

entries.summary: Advaita Vedanta, a school of Hindu philosophy associated with Shankara, teaches that the individual self (atman) is numerically identical with Brahman, the ultimate reality, and that liberation is the recognition of this nonduality. Other Hindu schools describe the relation between self and God differently. Their teaching is not summarised here until their sources are verified.
entries.origin: The identity of atman and Brahman is a central teaching of the Upanishads as interpreted in Advaita Vedanta. Hindu traditions vary in their account of Brahman.
entries.scripture: Scripture teaches that God created humans in his image (Genesis 1:27), and that the Creator is distinct from his creation (Isaiah 40:25; Romans 1:25). Humans are not God. Jesus is the eternal Son who is God (John 1:1; Colossians 2:9), and believers are adopted as children of God by grace (Galatians 4:5).

entries.summary: Latter-day Saint teaching distinguishes salvation from exaltation. The Church's essay Becoming Like God describes exaltation as the full inheritance of a child of God, available through the Atonement of Jesus Christ and by obedience to the laws and ordinances of the gospel, and says that the power of the Atonement is accessed through faith, repentance, baptism, the gift of the Holy Ghost and enduring to the end. The essay quotes the couplet 'As man now is, God once was: As God now is, man may be', and says that little has been revealed about its first half and that little is taught about it today.
entries.origin: The teaching of exaltation and of becoming like God comes from Joseph Smith and later Latter-day Saint leaders. The essay says that what the early church fathers meant by becoming God is open to interpretation, and that the biblical passages on human divine potential can be read in different ways.
entries.scripture: Scripture says there is one God, and that none was formed before or after him (Isaiah 43:10), and that beside him there is no God (Isaiah 44:6-8). Deuteronomy 6:4 declares that the LORD our God is one LORD, and John 4:24 says that God is Spirit. Believers are called children of God and heirs with Christ (Romans 8:16-17), and salvation is the free gift of God through Jesus Christ our Lord (Romans 6:23). Scripture says believers are to be conformed to the image of the Son (Romans 8:29). Protestant and Evangelical teaching holds that the Creator is distinct from his creatures, and that this conformity is to Christ in holiness and glory, not to becoming gods. The guide explains the Latter-day Saint teaching in its own terms before evaluating it.

entries.summary: Groups differ on how works relate to salvation, so each position is described separately. Jehovah's Witness teaching holds that works prove that living faith is present, and its official explanation says this 'does not mean that you can earn salvation'. It also teaches that a person who has been saved but fails to keep exercising faith could lose out on salvation. Latter-day Saint teaching, as stated in the Church's Gospel Topics essay Becoming Like God, holds that exaltation is available through the Atonement of Christ, by obedience to the laws and ordinances of the gospel. The Book of Mormon says that 'it is by grace that we are saved, after all we can do' (2 Nephi 25:23). Each position is explained in its own terms before it is evaluated.
entries.origin: These positions are distinct and should not be grouped together as one doctrine. Each is stated from its own publications.
entries.scripture: Scripture says: 'For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast' (Ephesians 2:8-9). Paul writes that a man is justified 'by faith without the deeds of the law' (Romans 3:28). Good works are the fruit of salvation and the evidence of living faith: 'Even so faith, if it hath not works, is dead, being alone' (James 2:17). The question to examine in each tradition is how it relates grace, faith, obedience, works, assurance and final salvation.

entries.summary: In many African traditional religions, the departed who are still remembered by name are spoken of as the living-dead. The scholar John Mbiti held that they remain in personal memory for as long as someone living remembers them by name. Not everyone who dies becomes an ancestor: many accounts say a person must have lived an exemplary life, and among various peoples a good death is also expected. The living-dead are believed to remain part of family life. They are thought to share in meals and libations, and to send dreams, warnings or instructions. Practices differ between peoples, families and regions, and many traditions also speak of a supreme God. Scholars disagree about whether honouring the dead is worship: Mbiti treats remembrance as a feature of social life rather than worship, and others describe it as worship. The guide distinguishes honouring and remembering the dead from invoking them, consulting them and making offerings to them, and it does not present one practice as the belief of all African peoples.
entries.origin: African traditional religions are many systems, not one, and the word ancestor covers several different ideas. Mbiti distinguished the departed who are still remembered by name from ancestors proper, who are no longer remembered individually. Idowu (1973) describes the ancestral cults as a means of communion and communication between the living and the spirit world of the ancestors. Among the Îgembe (Meru) community of Kenya, people often do not recall their ancestors' personal names, and the departed are remembered collectively rather than through a deep lineage; the study describes this as different from lineage-based peoples. A 2022 journal article on Kenyan history states that not everyone who dies becomes an ancestor, so the cult of the dead is not to be equated with the cult of the ancestors.
entries.scripture: Scripture commands honour for parents (Exodus 20:12) and names Christ as the one mediator between God and men (1 Timothy 2:5). It forbids consulting those with familiar spirits and wizards, and it forbids seeking the living's guidance from the dead (Leviticus 19:31; Deuteronomy 18:10-12; Isaiah 8:19-20). Scripture records that Saul died for asking counsel of one that had a familiar spirit (1 Chronicles 10:13). It teaches that after death comes judgment (Hebrews 9:27). Christians may honour and remember family members, and show them respect, without seeking their guidance or intercession. Christian prayer and worship are addressed to the triune God, and Christ is addressed in prayer as well (Acts 7:59; 1 Corinthians 1:2). Deuteronomy 18 condemns divination, consulting familiar spirits and necromancy; it is not to be used to condemn every act of cultural respect.

entries.summary: Three groups reject the Trinity in different ways. Oneness Pentecostal teaching, as stated on the official Our Beliefs page of the United Pentecostal Church International, is: 'There is one God, who has revealed Himself as Father; through His Son, in redemption; and as the Holy Spirit, by emanation.' That statement adds: 'Jesus Christ is God manifested in flesh.' Jehovah's Witness teaching holds that the Son is a created being and that the Holy Spirit is God's active force, not a person, and is subordinate to God. Latter-day Saint teaching holds that the Father, the Son and the Holy Ghost are three separate beings who make up the Godhead.
entries.origin: These are separate positions, each described from its own published teaching and not from the others. Historic Christian orthodoxy, as expressed in the Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed of 381, confesses one God and the deity of the Son, and confesses the Holy Spirit, who with the Father and the Son is worshipped and glorified. The Seventh-day Adventist Church also affirms one God in three coeternal Persons (Fundamental Belief 2).
entries.scripture: Scripture teaches the oneness of God: 'Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD' (Deuteronomy 6:4). The Father, Son and Holy Spirit are named together in the baptismal commission (Matthew 28:19). The Father and the Son are distinct and speak to each other (John 17:5), and the Father sends the Son and the Holy Spirit (John 14:16-17, 26). Against Oneness teaching, Scripture also shows the Son sharing glory with the Father before the world was (John 17:5) and is addressed as God (Hebrews 1:8). Against Jehovah's Witness teaching, the Son is called God (John 1:1; Hebrews 1:8), and the Spirit is spoken of as one who teaches, can be grieved and can be lied to (John 14:26; Ephesians 4:30; Acts 5:3-4). Against Latter-day Saint teaching, the Nicene Creed confesses one God, not three separate beings.

entries.summary: Jehovah's Witness teaching identifies Jesus with the archangel Michael and holds that Jesus is a created being, not the eternal God the Son. The Jehovah's Witness page 'The Archangel Michael, Who Is He?' says that Michael is 'evidently a name given to Jesus before and after his life on earth.' The Jehovah's Witness Bible Teach book Who Is Jesus Christ? says that Jesus 'was God's first creation' and that 'Jesus is the only one directly created by God'. Historic Christianity, as expressed in the Nicene Creed, confesses the Son as 'begotten, not made', and affirms his eternal deity.
entries.origin: This is Jehovah's Witness teaching. It rests on that group's reading of Daniel 10:13, Jude 9, 1 Thessalonians 4:16 and related passages, and on its rendering of Colossians 1:15 as 'the firstborn of all creation'.
entries.scripture: Scripture says that Jesus is the eternal Word who was God: 'In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was God... All things were made by him' (John 1:1-3). He is 'the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature: For by him were all things created' (Colossians 1:15-16). The KJV reads 'firstborn of every creature'; Jehovah's Witness publications read the word 'firstborn' as meaning the first thing created. Hebrews 1:5 asks: 'Unto which of the angels said he at any time, Thou art my Son, this day have I begotten thee?' Hebrews 1:6 says that God commands 'all the angels of God' to worship him. Jude 9 names Michael the archangel and does not say that Michael is Jesus. The identification rests on the wider Jehovah's Witness argument, which Hebrews 1 addresses.

entries.summary: Latter-day Saint teaching includes baptism for the dead, a proxy ordinance in which a living person is baptised on behalf of someone who has died. The Church's topic essay says the ordinance is an offer, and that the validity of a proxy baptism depends on the deceased person accepting it. The Church cites 1 Corinthians 15:29 as evidence that baptisms for the dead were done in Paul's time.
entries.origin: This is a Latter-day Saint practice performed in temples. The Church's doctrinal basis is that God has prepared a way for all people to receive the blessings of baptism.
entries.scripture: Scripture teaches that people believe and are baptised in this life in response to the gospel (Mark 16:16; Acts 2:38). In 1 Corinthians 15:29 Paul mentions baptism for the dead without commending the practice or commanding it, and its meaning is disputed among commentators, so it cannot bear the weight of a saving ordinance. Mark 16:9-20 is a passage whose authenticity is disputed, so Mark 16:16 is not the main proof. Hebrews 9:27 says that death is followed by judgment, which is consistent with the decision being made in this life, though it does not address proxy ordinances directly. The clearer New Testament call is to repentance and faith now: God 'now commandeth all men every where to repent' (Acts 17:30), and 'now is the accepted time' (2 Corinthians 6:2).

entries.summary: Seventh-day Adventists are Trinitarian. Their Fundamental Belief 2 states that there is one God: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, a unity of three coeternal Persons. They keep the seventh day, Saturday, as the Sabbath. Their Fundamental Belief 20 describes the seventh-day Sabbath as a day of rest, worship and ministry. Their Fundamental Belief 13 describes the remnant as keeping the commandments of God and the faith of Jesus. A 2021 Biblical Research Institute answer, published in the General Conference Executive Committee Newsletter, describes Sunday observance as a distinguishing sign in the end-time test, and does not settle whether Sunday worship marks a person before that test. The guide does not say that present-day Sunday worshippers are condemned or bear the mark.
entries.origin: This is Seventh-day Adventist teaching on the Sabbath and on the end-time test. Individual Adventists and local congregations vary in how they apply it, and the guide does not describe any individual's standing before God.
entries.scripture: Colossians 2:16-17 says: 'Let no man therefore judge you in meat, or in drink, or in respect of an holyday, or of the new moon, or of the sabbath days.' Romans 14:5-6 says that each should be fully persuaded in his own mind, and that he who regardeth the day regardeth it unto the Lord. Adventist readers rely on Revelation 14:12, which speaks of those 'that keep the commandments of God, and the faith of Jesus', and read the seventh-day Sabbath as the sign of loyalty. Readers who do not regard the Sabbath commandment as binding on Christians point to Christ's word that the Son of man is Lord also of the sabbath (Mark 2:28), and to the first Christians' gatherings on the first day of the week (Acts 20:7; 1 Corinthians 16:2).

entries.summary: New Age teaching is a diverse movement, not one doctrine. Britannica describes it as a body of diverse believers united by a few ideas, with strongest roots in modern esotericism and in Helena Blavatsky's Theosophical Society. Its practices include healing and self-transformation, and meditation. Because the movement has no single doctrine, the guide does not attribute to New Age writers as a whole any specific teaching about energy.
entries.origin: The movement has roots in modern esotericism and in Theosophy, and its strands differ in origin and emphasis. They should not be presented as one teaching.
entries.scripture: Scripture teaches that God is Spirit (John 4:24). Healing is sought from God in prayer (James 5:14-15). Believers are told to test every spirit (1 John 4:1). Scripture forbids divination and the seeking of guidance from the occult (Deuteronomy 18:10-12). Christians may evaluate any practice or teaching by these tests, and the guide explains each New Age claim in its own terms before doing so.

entries.summary: Christian Science, founded by Mary Baker Eddy in 1866, describes itself as based on the Bible and the teachings of Christ Jesus. Its religious tenet 5 states: 'We acknowledge that the crucifixion of Jesus and his resurrection served to uplift faith to understand eternal Life, even the allness of Soul, Spirit, and the nothingness of matter.' Christian Science therefore affirms the crucifixion and resurrection as part of its teaching, but interprets them differently from the historic Christian confession of Christ's bodily resurrection. Its FAQ says that, while it affirms the divinity of the Christ, it does not equate Jesus with God. Its FAQ lists Mind among seven synonymous names for God. It teaches that spiritual healing, as taught by Christ Jesus, is accessible to anyone today, and says that Christian Scientists are free to choose their own form of healthcare, including medical care.
entries.origin: Christian Science was founded by Mary Baker Eddy. Its main text is Science and Health with Key to the Scriptures, where its six tenets appear on pages 496-497 according to its official site.
entries.scripture: Scripture presents Jesus as a real man who was born, suffered, died and rose bodily: 'Behold my hands and my feet, that it is I myself: handle me, and see; for a spirit hath not flesh and bones, as ye see me have' (Luke 24:39). Paul writes that Christ 'died for our sins according to the scriptures' and 'rose again the third day according to the scriptures' (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). Scripture also says that 'the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us' (John 1:14), and that God saw everything he had made, and 'behold, it was very good' (Genesis 1:31). The Son is God (John 1:1; Colossians 2:9). Christian healing is by God's power through prayer and faith (James 5:14-16), and redemption is through the blood of Christ (Ephesians 1:7). The guide describes Christian Science's own interpretation before evaluating it.

entries.summary: Secular and non-religious worldviews differ, and the guide describes the specific one a person holds. Atheism, in the standard philosophical sense, is the proposition that God does not exist. Agnosticism is not one claim. In one sense, an agnostic holds that neither theism nor atheism is known; in another, that neither is true. Naturalism has two components that must be kept apart. Ontological naturalism, as the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy states it, holds that reality has no place for supernatural or other spooky kinds of entity, and that the mental, biological and social realms are nothing more than arrangements of physical entities. Methodological naturalism is concerned with ways of investigating reality, and is a separate matter. The Stanford Encyclopedia notes that atheism and naturalism are not identical. Humanist Manifesto III describes humanism as a progressive philosophy of life that, without supernaturalism, affirms our ability and responsibility to lead ethical lives, and it holds that ethical values are derived from human need and interest as tested by experience.
entries.origin: Atheism, agnosticism, naturalism, secular humanism and related views have different histories and should not be treated as one position. The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy distinguishes the psychological and epistemological senses of agnosticism.
entries.scripture: Psalm 19:1 says that the heavens declare the glory of God. Romans 1:20 says that God's invisible things, even his eternal power and Godhead, are clearly seen through the things that are made, so that people are without excuse. Romans 2:14-15 says that the work of the law is written in human hearts. Acts 17:11 commends those who searched the scriptures daily to test what they heard. Faith and reason are not opposed in Scripture, and the guide treats the reasons a person gives as worth examining on their merits.

entries.summary: Islamic teaching holds that Jesus, son of Mary, was not crucified. Muslim commentators have generally read the Qur'an's passage on the crucifixion as denying that it took place. The best-known classical explanation is that God made another person resemble Jesus, so that this person was crucified in his place while Jesus was taken up to God. Commentators give different accounts of who was crucified and how, so the guide describes the common reading and does not present one account as settled. A small minority of scholars, past and present, have read the passage differently. This entry covers the classical reading only and does not set out later reinterpretations of what happened to Jesus afterwards. The guide describes this teaching in its own words and does not quote the Qur'an.
entries.origin: The teaching rests on one passage of the Qur'an (Surah 4, verses 157 and 158) and its interpretation in Muslim commentary. Al-Tabari sets out several accounts of the resemblance and prefers the account in which it was cast over everyone in the house with Jesus. Ibn Kathir gives the account, traced to Ibn Abbas, of a young companion who volunteered to take Jesus's appearance and was crucified in his place. A 2023 article in the American Journal of Islam and Society reviews the long-standing reading and the recent minority challenge to it.
entries.scripture: The New Testament records that Jesus was crucified and died. Matthew 27:50 and John 19:33-35 report his death, and John 19:35 gives the testimony of an eyewitness. Paul's summary of the gospel names Christ's death, his burial, his rising on the third day, and the many witnesses who saw him afterwards (1 Corinthians 15:3-8). Peter and Paul preached a crucified and risen Messiah (Acts 2:23; 1 Corinthians 1:23). Scripture is the final authority here, and its eyewitness testimony conflicts with the denial that Jesus was crucified. Christians also weigh the historical evidence together with the meaning of the cross, which they hold is the ground of atonement.

entries.summary: Islamic teaching holds that God has no children, and that Jesus, son of Mary, was a messenger and not God. Surah 112 rejects the idea that God has children or was ever born. Other passages say that Jesus is the Messiah and a messenger like those before him, warn Christians against going to extremes about him, and reject the belief that God is one of three. Muslims honour Jesus as the Messiah, a prophet and a servant of God, but reject the Christian confession that he is God the Son. The guide describes this teaching in its own words and does not quote the Qur'an.
entries.origin: This is the teaching of Islam, based on the Qur'an. Ibn Kathir reads Surah 112, which describes God as al-Samad, as rejecting the idea that God begets or was begotten. Al-Tabari reads the Surah 4 passage as addressing those who call Jesus God's son and as rejecting that claim, since God does not take a son. Ibn Kathir (abridged) reads the passages on Jesus as a servant of God and not his son in the same way. The guide describes these as the common Muslim reading in general terms, drawn from the commentary openings checked so far; it does not present any one commentator's full treatment of these verses as settled.
entries.scripture: Scripture teaches that the Son is eternal and is God. John 1:1-14 presents the Word as God, who became flesh, and Hebrews 1:2-3 presents the Son as the one through whom God made the worlds and the exact image of God's person. Jesus said, "I and my Father are one" (John 10:30). Christians hold that the Father's begetting of the Son is eternal and not physical, as the Nicene Creed affirms, and 1 Timothy 2:5 calls Jesus the one mediator between God and men. Islam honours Jesus as Messiah and prophet while rejecting his divine Sonship. Scripture's witness is that he is the eternal Son and God.

entries.summary: The Protestant and Evangelical Bible contains 66 books: 39 in the Old Testament and 27 in the New. The Westminster Confession (1646) states that the books commonly called Apocrypha, not being of divine inspiration, are no part of the canon of the Scripture. The Catholic canon, as set out by the Council of Trent (Session 4, 1546), receives Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach (Ecclesiasticus), Baruch and the two books of the Maccabees among the Old Testament books, and receives the Old Testament books entire with all their parts, as contained in the old Latin Vulgate. Orthodox churches do not share one universal list in every detail. Philip Schaff's English summary of the 1672 Synod of Jerusalem reports that the Synod defines the canon as including the Apocrypha, and his summary names Tobit, Judith, Wisdom and Sirach among them. Schaff also reports that the confession of Metrophanes Critopulus mentions only twenty-two canonical books of the Old Testament. These differences concern reception and authority, and this guide presents the Protestant and Catholic arguments as arguments about reception and authority.
entries.origin: The 66-book canon was recognised through the church's reception of apostolic books and of the Old Testament books that Jesus and the apostles cited as Scripture. The Catholic canon was defined at the Council of Trent. Lists differ across Christian history, and some boundaries were debated.
entries.scripture: Scripture is given by inspiration of God (2 Timothy 3:16), and Peter counts Paul's letters with the other Scriptures (2 Peter 3:15-16). Jesus and the apostles treated the Old Testament writings as Scripture, including the phrase 'the law of Moses, and in the prophets, and in the psalms' (Luke 24:44). That phrase names the divisions of the Hebrew Scriptures but does not itself list every book. Deuteronomy 4:2 and Revelation 22:18-19 warn against adding to or taking from God's words, but each passage is read in its own context and does not by itself fix the number of books. The Protestant argument is historical: the church received these 66 books as God's words, and the additional books are read for history and edification. The Catholic argument is that the church's councils defined the wider canon. Both are arguments about reception and authority, and the guide presents them as such.

entries.summary: A question asks whether a named church or group is true, saved, or a cult. The guide describes that institution's official, publicly documented teaching accurately and evaluates it against Scripture. Where an institution's official teaching contradicts Scripture and historic orthodox Christianity, the guide says so plainly, explains the contradiction and its doctrinal consequences. The guide does not decide the salvation of any individual adherent, does not assign guilt to members, and does not use the word cult as an unsupported label.

entries.scripture: Scripture is the standard for every teaching (Isaiah 8:20; Acts 17:11). The guide tests an institution's official teaching against Scripture, so that a clear contradiction of Scripture is named as such. The judgment of any person's heart belongs to God (1 Samuel 16:7; Romans 14:12), so the guide does not decide any individual's eternal destiny.

entries.summary: A question names a religious group, such as Latter-day Saints, Jehovah's Witnesses, Seventh-day Adventists, Oneness Pentecostals, Christian Science, Christadelphians, the Catholic Church or the Eastern Orthodox churches. The guide describes the group's official teaching from its own published sources, keeps apart official teaching, historical teaching, local practice and individual belief, and then evaluates the official teaching against Scripture. The Catholic Church and the Eastern Orthodox churches confess the Nicene faith: one God, and in one Lord Jesus Christ the only-begotten Son of God, begotten of the Father before all worlds, very God of very God, begotten, not made, who for us men, and for our salvation, came down from heaven, and was made man. The guide states their differences from the Perazim framework specifically, and points to the entries on those differences, such as purgatory, saint prayer, Marian titles, icons and the canon.

Where a group's own published sources could be read, the guide uses them for that group's official teaching; where a point rests on a secondary source, the group entry says so. It separates an institution's official teaching from local practice and individual belief, and it gives no verdict on any member's eternal destiny.
